yield.src: USDA Table of Cooking Yields for Meat and Poultry (USDA ARS Nutrient Data Laboratory, Dec 2012), https://www.ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/80400525/Data/retn/USDA_CookingYields_MeatPoultry.pdf: "Chicken, broiler-fryer, breast", baked/roasted 72% (min 61, max 82; AH-102 1975 data). name: Chicken thighs, boneless skinless — roasted (cooked weight)
src: Calculated: USDA FDC 2646171 (Foundation Foods, published 10/26/2023) "Chicken, thigh, boneless, skinless, raw" ÷ cooked yield 0.75, assuming all protein and fat stay in the meat (so it errs slightly high). USDA's older analytical roasted value (FDC 172388: 179 kcal, 24.8 P, 8.2 F) is lower; the matching older SR raw thigh (FDC 173627) has 4.1 g fat/100 g vs 7.9 g in the Foundation retail sample, so the old cooked value likely under-reads today's thighs by about 10%.

yield.src: Bognár A. (2002) Tables on weight yield of food and retention factors of food constituents for the calculation of nutrient composition of cooked foods (dishes). BFE-R--02-03, Bundesforschungsanstalt für Ernährung, Karlsruhe, https://publikationen.bibliothek.kit.edu/9642002/1928, Table 13: "Fish, fillet (cod, red fish, pollack), fried" (pan, deep-fried or grilled) 0.80 ± 0.02 (n=10). No salmon-specific yield was found in USDA or Bognár; this lean-fish fillet value is the closest sourced number.

check.method: (raw P×4.27×0.95 + raw F×9.02×0.8) ÷ yield; retention factors: Bognár 2002 Table 22 (fat fish >5% fat), "fry in oven", fish part: protein 0.95, fat 0.80

logAs: raw weight — cut the fillet into portions raw on prep day (fish values shift with cooking more than meat)
note: Counts as the day's omega-3. Bognár's fat-fish factors assume about 20% of the fat leaves the fillet in the oven, so logging the raw weight counts that fat too (errs slightly high, which is the safe side).
